newsitem.title: GERMANY: SOCCER SHOWCASE-MUNICH'S LIONS HOPE TO ROAR AGAIN.
newsitem.headline: SOCCER SHOWCASE-MUNICH'S LIONS HOPE TO ROAR AGAIN.

text.p: When the Bundesliga was founded in 1963, there was only one team worth talking about in Munich.

1860 Munich, nicknamed "the Lions", had a huge following and a strong working-class tradition. Bayern Munich were nothing more than a promising regional league side with a reputation for snobbery and pretension.
But on the pitch Bayern soon caught up and left their local rivals trailing hopelessly in their wake.
So when the two sides meet, as in this Sunday's Bundesliga derby match, history and pride play as big a role as points.
"We really were nobodies," Franz Beckenbauer, who began his career in Bayern in 1964, recalls in his autobiography. "1860 had a huge advantage when it came to experience and popularity."
Beckenbauer, now club president at Bayern, tells one story which sums up the relationship between the two clubs in those days.
Once, a Bayern game was moved from the stadium the teams shared just before kick-off. The reason? "It suddenly occurred to someone it would be better to preserve the pitch for the Lions."

Times have changed. Bayern, with a team including the likes of Beckenbauer, Gerd Mueller and Sepp Maier, set new standards of excellence in German soccer from the late 1960s onwards, laying the foundations for 13 Bundesliga titles and three European Cup triumphs.
The club moved into the city's Olympic Stadium in the early 1970s, giving them the perfect platform on which to showcase their skills.
1860, meanwhile, began a catastrophic descent worsened by years of mismanagement.
The club plummeted all the way to regional soccer and endured its nadir in 1985, finishing in 11th place in the Bavarian league as Bayern won their eighth Bundesliga title.
Things began to change at 1860 when current president Karl-Heinz Wildmoser took control in 1992.

The burly Bavarian restaurateur dragged the club into the modern era, investing in players and facilities and persuading supporters it was time to move away from their Gruenwald Strasse ground and share the Olympic Stadium with Bayern.
1860 returned to the Bundesliga in 1994 and have made steady progress since then, finishing 14th in their first season and eighth in their second. They stand sixth at the moment.

Now their aim is a return to European competition -- a goal which revives memories of the club's golden era when they reached the 1965 Cup Winners' Cup final, losing to West Ham of England in front of 98,000 spectators at Wembley.
"We'll be happy if we can establish ourselves in the top half of the Bundesliga, somewhere between third and eighth place," Wildmoser said. "This city has enough potential for two top-class clubs."

The president says 1860 do not want to replace Bayern as Germany's top club but some 1860 fanatics still harbour the dream of a return to the days when upstarts such as Beckenbauer played second fiddle to the Lions.
"You just have to look at Milan," said veteran 1860 defender Thomas Miller, a survivor from the regional league days. "Two years ago, AC Milan were way ahead, now they're clearly behind Inter."
